title: And, or and not
objectives: Build compound statements with and, or and not, and check them with a truth table.

screens.title: A price alert
screens.prose: A share's closing price and volume over one week. An alert fires on a day when **the price is above £100 and volume is above 1 million**.
screens.question: Tap the days on which the alert fires.

hints.text: Check each day twice: once for the price, once for the volume.
Wednesday's price passes, but look at its volume.
Mon and Thu pass both tests. Tue fails on price, Wed on volume, Fri on both.

feedback.correct: Mon and Thu: the only days that pass both tests.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A day counts only if it passes both tests.

byKey.price-only: You kept Wednesday, which passes on price only. Its volume, 0.7 million, is not above 1 million.
byKey.volume-only: You kept Tuesday, which passes on volume only. Its price, £98, is not above £100.
byKey.r1: Tuesday's volume passes, but its price of £98 does not.
byKey.r2: Wednesday's price passes, but its volume of 0.7 million does not.

explain.text: With **and**, a day must pass both tests. Only Monday and Thursday do.

screens.title: Change one word
screens.prose: Now the alert fires when **the price is above £100 or volume is above 1 million**.
screens.question: Tap the days on which the alert fires now.

hints.text: A day fires if it passes at least one test.
Monday passes both tests. Does that stop it passing at least one?
Mon, Tue, Wed and Thu each pass at least one test. Fri passes neither.

feedback.correct: Mon, Tue, Wed and Thu. Only Friday passes neither test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A day fires when it passes one test or both.

byKey.exclusive: You left out Mon and Thu, which pass both tests. Passing both still counts as passing one.
byKey.and: You kept only the days that pass both tests. With **or**, one test is enough.
byKey.r4: Friday fails both tests: £97 and 0.8 million.
byKey.r0: Monday passes both tests, so it passes at least one.
byKey.r3: Thursday passes both tests, so it passes at least one.

explain.text: With **or**, one passing test is enough, and two are fine too. Four days fire; only Friday fails both.

canvas.caption: Fires with **or**: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu

screens.title: Not
screens.prose: A second alert fires when **the price is not above £100**.
screens.question: Tap the days on which the second alert fires.

hints.text: Which days have a price of £100 or less?
Look at the price column only.
Tue at £98 and Fri at £97 are not above £100.

feedback.correct: Tue and Fri. On every other day the price is above £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the days whose price is £100 or less.

byKey.above: You tapped the days whose price is above £100. **Not** flips the test, so it keeps the other days.

explain.text: **Not** keeps exactly the days the price test rejects. Those are Tuesday and Friday.

screens.title: Truth tables
screens.prose: Let $P$ be “the price is above £100” and $Q$ be “volume is above 1 million”. We write $P \land Q$ for **and**, $P \lor Q$ for **or**, and $\lnot P$ for **not**. Each row below is one way $P$ and $Q$ can turn out.

state.caption: This week's days, as values of $P$ and $Q$

screens.question: Fill in the columns for $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q$.

hints.text: Use the days: Monday is the row where $P$ and $Q$ are both T.
Did the **and** alert fire on Monday? Did the **or** alert?
$P \land Q$ is T only on the T, T row. $P \lor Q$ is F only on the F, F row.

feedback.correct: $P \land Q$ is true on one row; $P \lor Q$ is false on one row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each row as a day and ask whether the alert fired.

byKey.r0c3: You put F for $P \lor Q$ when both are true. Monday passes both tests, and the **or** alert fired.
byKey.r1c2: On the T, F row only the price test passes. **And** needs both.
byKey.r2c2: On the F, T row only the volume test passes. **And** needs both.
byKey.r3c3: On the F, F row neither test passes, so **or** fails too.

explain.text: $P \land Q$ is true only when both parts are true. $P \lor Q$ is false only when both parts are false. Monday and Thursday are the T, T row; Friday is the F, F row.

screens.title: Truth sets
screens.prose: Each circle holds the days on which its statement is true. Every day sits in exactly one region.

params.universe: Five days. P: price above £100. Q: volume above 1m.

screens.question: Tap the region where $P \land Q$ is true.

hints.text: $P \land Q$ needs a day inside both circles.
Only one region is inside both circles.
The overlap holds Mon and Thu, the days the **and** alert fired.

feedback.correct: The overlap: Mon and Thu, inside both circles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the region inside both circles.

byKey.A: Wednesday is inside $P$ only. Its volume test fails.
byKey.B: Tuesday is inside $Q$ only. Its price test fails.
byKey.none: Friday is outside both circles, so both tests fail there.

explain.text: $P \land Q$ is true exactly in the overlap of the two circles. That region holds Monday and Thursday.

screens.title: The truth set of or

params.universe: Five days. P: price above £100. Q: volume above 1m.

screens.question: Tap every region where $P \lor Q$ is true.

hints.text: $P \lor Q$ needs a day inside at least one circle.
The overlap is inside both circles. Is it inside at least one?
Every region except the outside: $P$ only, both, and $Q$ only.

feedback.correct: Everything inside the circles: Mon, Tue, Wed and Thu.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every region inside at least one circle.

byKey.exclusive: You left out the overlap. Days in both circles are in at least one, so **or** holds there.
byKey.overlap: You kept the overlap only. That is $P \land Q$; **or** needs just one circle.
byKey.none: Friday's region is outside both circles, so $P \lor Q$ is false there.

explain.text: $P \lor Q$ is true anywhere inside the circles, the overlap included. Only the outside region, Friday, makes it false.

screens.title: Two ways to say not both
screens.prose: “It is not the case that both tests pass” is $\lnot(P \land Q)$. “The price test fails or the volume test fails” is $(\lnot P) \lor (\lnot Q)$.

params.universe: Five days. P: price above £100. Q: volume above 1m.

screens.question: Fill in both columns.

hints.text: For the third column, take your $P \land Q$ column and flip every value.
For the last column, write $\lnot P$ and $\lnot Q$ for the row first, then apply **or**.
On the T, F row, $\lnot P$ is F and $\lnot Q$ is T, so the **or** is T.

feedback.correct: Both columns read F, T, T, T. They agree on every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work row by row: negate first, then combine.

byKey.r1c3: You put F on the T, F row. There $\lnot Q$ is T, and **or** needs only one true part.
byKey.r0c2: On the T, T row $P \land Q$ is T, so its negation is F.
byKey.r0c3: On the T, T row $\lnot P$ and $\lnot Q$ are both F, so the **or** is F.

explain.text: Both columns are F on the T, T row and T on the other three. So $\lnot(P \land Q)$ and $(\lnot P) \lor (\lnot Q)$ say the same thing. On the diagram, both are true everywhere outside the overlap.

canvas.caption: Shaded: where both forms are true

screens.title: Tea or coffee
screens.prose: A waiter asks “tea or coffee?” and means one, not both. A colleague reads the alert's **or** the same way.
screens.question: Which column, read top to bottom, is $P \lor Q$ in maths?

options.why: You left out the T, T row. In maths $P \lor Q$ is true when both hold, so the alert fires on Mon and Thu too.
That is $P \land Q$, which needs both parts. **Or** needs only one.
That is “neither”, true only when both parts fail. It is $\lnot(P \lor Q)$.

hints.text: Is Monday, where both tests pass, an alert day under **or**?
The first row is the T, T row.
In maths **or** is inclusive: it is T on the T, T row. Only the F, F row is F.

feedback.correct: T, T, T, F. The maths **or** includes the case where both hold.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide the T, T row first.

byKey.excl: You left out the T, T row: the waiter's **or**. In maths $P \lor Q$ is true when both hold, so Mon and Thu fire too.

explain.text: In maths, $P \lor Q$ means at least one of the two, so it is T on the T, T row. The waiter's “one but not both” is a different connective, the exclusive or.

screens.title: Check every row in code
screens.prose: Two statements in $P$ and $Q$ say the same thing when their truth tables agree on all four rows. In Python, `True` and `False` stand for T and F. A loop over `(True, False)` twice visits every row. Four rows is every case, so here checking them all is a proof.
screens.question: Write `same_truth_table(f, g)`. It returns `True` when `f(p, q) == g(p, q)` on all four rows, and `False` otherwise.

examples.setup: f = lambda p, q: not (p and q); g = lambda p, q: (not p) or (not q)

tests.setup: f = lambda p, q: not (p and q); g = lambda p, q: (not p) or (not q)
f = lambda p, q: not (p and q); g = lambda p, q: (not p) and (not q)
f = lambda p, q: p or q; g = lambda p, q: q or p
f = lambda p, q: (not p) or q; g = lambda p, q: (not q) or p
f = lambda p, q: p or q; g = lambda p, q: True
f = lambda p, q: p; g = lambda p, q: q
f = lambda p, q: p; g = lambda p, q: p or (p and q)

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each one defines `f` and `g` with `lambda` and expects exactly `True` or `False`.

hints.text: Two `for` loops, one inside the other, visit the four rows.
Inside the loops, `return False` as soon as `f(p, q) != g(p, q)`. After both loops finish, `return True`.

feedback.correct: Your loops visit all four rows, so a `True` from your function settles the question.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test: which row did your code miss?

byKey.test-5: Test 5 differs only on the last row, where both inputs are `False`. Check your loops reach it.

screens.title: De Morgan's law
screens.prose:
Your two columns agreed on every row. That is **De Morgan's law**:

$$\lnot(P \land Q) \text{ has the same truth table as } (\lnot P) \lor (\lnot Q)$$

To negate an **and**, negate each part and switch to **or**. Level 2 proves the same law for sets.
screens.question: By the same reasoning, which has the same truth table as $\lnot(P \lor Q)$?

options.why: You negated the parts but kept **or**. On the T, F row $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ is F, while this is T.
You switched the connective but did not negate the parts. On the T, T row this is T, but $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ is F.
You negated only $P$. On the F, T row this is T, but $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ is F.

feedback.correct: Right. “Not either” is “neither”: not $P$ and not $Q$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate each part and switch the connective.

byKey.or: You kept **or**. Negating an **or** switches it to **and**, just as negating an **and** switched it to **or**.

explain.text: $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ is true only on the F, F row. $(\lnot P) \land (\lnot Q)$ is true only there too. This is the second De Morgan law.

screens.title: A risk flag
screens.prose: A risk system flags a trade if **it is over £1 million or the counterparty is unrated**. Fill in the flag for each trade, using T and F.
screens.question: Which trades are flagged?

hints.text: For each trade, ask: is it over £1 million, or unrated, or both?
Trade A is both over £1 million and unrated.
A, B and C pass at least one test. D passes neither.

feedback.correct: A, B and C are flagged; D is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flag a trade that passes at least one test.

byKey.r0c3: You left trade A unflagged, the one that passes both tests. Reading **or** as one but not both misses the biggest risk on the sheet.
byKey.r3c3: Trade D is £0.6m with a rated counterparty. It passes neither test.

explain.text: Trades A, B and C pass at least one test, so the inclusive **or** flags all three. A junior who reads **or** as exclusive would miss trade A, which is large and unrated.

ideas: $P \land Q$ is true only when both parts are true. $P \lor Q$ is false only when both parts are false. $\lnot P$ flips the value of $P$.
A truth table lists every row: 4 for two letters, 8 for three. Two statements say the same thing when their columns agree on every row.
De Morgan's law: $\lnot(P \land Q)$ agrees with $(\lnot P) \lor (\lnot Q)$, and $\lnot(P \lor Q)$ with $(\lnot P) \land (\lnot Q)$.

formula.name: De Morgan's law
formula.note: To negate an **and**, negate each part and switch to **or**.

summary.trap: In maths **or** is inclusive: $P \lor Q$ is true when both parts are true.

quiz.prose: A colleague writes $\lnot(P \land Q)$ as $(\lnot P) \land (\lnot Q)$.
quiz.question: On how many of the four rows do the two columns agree?

widget.label: Rows that agree
widget.accept: 2: the T, T row and the F, F row

feedback.correct: 2 of 4. The middle rows disagree, so the forms are not the same.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the last two columns row by row.

byKey.all: You took the forms to agree everywhere. The T, F and F, T rows differ.
byKey.one: Check the first row too: both columns are F there.

explain.text: The columns agree on the T, T row (both F) and the F, F row (both T). They differ on the two middle rows. Negating an **and** needs an **or**.

quiz.prose: A statement is built from three letters, $P$, $Q$ and $R$. Each letter can be T or F.
quiz.question: How many rows does its truth table need?

feedback.correct: 8. Each new letter doubles the rows: $2^3 = 8$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two letters gave 4 rows. What does a third letter do?

byKey.times: You multiplied 3 by 2. Each letter doubles the count, so it is $2 \times 2 \times 2$.
byKey.square: You worked out $3^2$. There are 2 values for each of 3 letters: $2^3$.
byKey.add: You added. Each of the 4 rows for $P$ and $Q$ splits in two for $R$.

explain.text: Each row for $P$ and $Q$ splits into two, one with $R$ true and one with $R$ false. So 4 rows become $2 \times 4 = 8$.

quiz.prose: Look at $P \lor \lnot P$ and $P \land \lnot P$. Each has a two-row truth table.
quiz.question: Which description is right?

options.text: $P \lor \lnot P$ is T on both rows; $P \land \lnot P$ is F on both
$P \lor \lnot P$ is F on both rows; $P \land \lnot P$ is T on both
options.why: You swapped them. One of $P$ and $\lnot P$ is always T, so their **or** is always T.

options.text: Both depend on whether $P$ is T
options.why: You expected the value to follow $P$. On each row exactly one of $P$, $\lnot P$ is T, so the results never change.

options.text: Both are T on both rows
options.why: You treated **and** like **or**. $P$ and $\lnot P$ are never both T.

feedback.correct: Right. The first is a **tautology** and the second a **contradiction**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the two rows for each one.

explain.text: On each row exactly one of $P$ and $\lnot P$ is true. So their **or** is always T, a tautology, and their **and** is always F, a contradiction.

quiz.prose: Back to the rule “flag a trade if it is over £1 million or the counterparty is unrated”. A junior reads **or** as one but not both.
quiz.question: Which kind of trade would the junior wrongly leave unflagged?

options.text: Over £1 million with an unrated counterparty
Over £1 million with a rated counterparty
options.why: That trade passes exactly one test, so both readings flag it.

options.text: Under £1 million with an unrated counterparty
options.why: That trade passes exactly one test, so both readings flag it.

options.text: Under £1 million with a rated counterparty
options.why: That trade passes neither test, so neither reading flags it.

feedback.correct: Right. The trade that passes both tests is the one the exclusive reading drops.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the trade where the two readings disagree.

explain.text: The exclusive reading drops only the T, T row. That is the trade that is large and unrated, the riskiest kind.
